title: About Me
text:
I am Daniel Soto
I am an incoming M.S. student at Northwestern University’s Engineering and Applied Mathematics (ESAM) program. I have a dual major in Mathematics (B.S.) and Linguistics (B.A.) from the University of Florida, along with a minor in Statistics.
I have applied my skills in a diverse set of projects. at the University of Florida, I contributed to a project involving Linguistic Indicators of Hoarding Disorder. At the Summer Internship in Biostatistics and Data Science (SIBDS), I helped analyze risk factors contributing to weapon-carrying behavior, and also assessed the benefits of soluble corn fiber supplements towards aiding bone development in teens.
I am deeply invested in mathematical modeling and computational modeling: I am eager to find areas in our lives where we can apply modeling to solve complex problems. I also enjoy data science, applying statistics and machine learning techniques to reveal insights and patterns among many types of data.
I am also dedicated to ensuring clarity and reproducibility in my work, using tools like Quarto and RMarkdown. This approach ensures that my research is trustworthy and easily followed by others.

title: Data and Research Question
text:
The Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS) is a national survey that monitors health-related behaviors among high school students, including weapon carrying and associated risk factors.



Source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
Year: 2023
Target Population: High school students
Sample Size: Approximately 19,000 students nationwide




How do logistic regression, lasso, k-nearest neighbors, and tree-based models compare in predicting school-based weapon carrying among adolescents based on risk and protective factors?



The dataset includes information on various health-related behaviors:

Outcome

Weapon Carrying (Carried a weapon on school property)

Predictors

Traumatic experiences
School Safety Perceptions
Bullying Experiences
Family Support
Social Media Use
Peer Relationships






library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(dissertationData)
library(here)
data(clean_yrbs_2023)





analysis_data <- clean_yrbs_2023 %>%
    select(
        WeaponCarryingSchool, AttackedInNeighborhood, Bullying,
        SexualAbuseByOlderPerson, ParentalPhysicalAbuse, ParentSubstanceUse,
        ParentIncarceration, SchoolConnectedness, ParentalMonitoring,
        UnfairDisciplineAtSchool, Homelessness
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(WeaponCarryingSchool)) %>%
    mutate(across(
        c(
            ParentSubstanceUse, ParentIncarceration, SchoolConnectedness,
            ParentalMonitoring, UnfairDisciplineAtSchool
        ),
        ~ as.numeric(.x) - 1
    )) %>%
    mutate(across(
        c(
            ParentSubstanceUse, ParentIncarceration, SchoolConnectedness,
            ParentalMonitoring, UnfairDisciplineAtSchool
        ),
        ~ factor(.x)
    ))





set.seed(1990)

analysis_split <- initial_split(analysis_data,
    strata = WeaponCarryingSchool
)

analysis_train <- training(analysis_split)
analysis_test <- testing(analysis_split)

analysis_split

title: Lasso Regression
text:
Lasso regression is a statistical model that combines linear/logistic regression with L1 regularization to perform both variable selection and regularization. The term “Lasso” stands for “Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator.” This method is particularly useful when dealing with datasets that have many predictors, as it helps to: - Reduce overfitting by penalizing large coefficients - Perform automatic feature selection by shrinking some coefficients to exactly zero - Handle multicollinearity by selecting only one variable from a group of highly correlated predictors
In this analysis, we’ll use Lasso regression to predict weapon carrying behavior in schools, demonstrating how this method can help identify the most important predictors while maintaining model interpretability.

title: Lasso Regression
text:
Setting Up the Environment
First, we need to load the necessary packages for our analysis. We’ll use tidymodels for modeling, tidyverse for data manipulation, and here for consistent file paths.

library(here)
library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)

title: Lasso Regression
text:
Loading the Data
We’ll work with pre-processed data sets that have been split into training and test sets, along with cross-validation folds. These files are stored in the processed_data directory.

analysis_data <- readRDS(here("models", "data", "analysis_data.rds"))
analysis_train <- readRDS(here("models", "data", "analysis_train.rds"))
analysis_test <- readRDS(here("models","data", "analysis_test.rds"))
analysis_folds <- readRDS(here("models", "data", "analysis_folds.rds"))

title: Lasso Regression
text:
Data Preprocessing
Before fitting our model, we need to preprocess the data. We’ll create a recipe that: - Imputes missing values in categorical variables using the mode - Imputes missing values in numeric variables using the mean - Removes predictors with zero variance - Removes highly correlated predictors (correlation threshold = 0.7) - Creates dummy variables for categorical predictors

weapon_carry_recipe <- 
  recipe(formula = WeaponCarryingSchool ~ ., data = analysis_train) |>
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_mean(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |> 
  step_corr(all_numeric_predictors(), threshold = 0.7) %>% 
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

weapon_carry_recipe

title: Lasso Regression
text:
Model Specification
We’ll use a logistic regression model with Lasso regularization. The Lasso (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) helps with feature selection by penalizing the absolute size of coefficients. We set mixture = 1 to specify a pure Lasso model, and we’ll tune the penalty parameter to find the optimal level of regularization.

weapon_carry_spec <-
  logistic_reg(penalty = tune(), 
               mixture = 1) |> 
  set_engine('glmnet')

weapon_carry_spec

Logistic Regression Model Specification (classification)

  penalty = tune()
  mixture = 1

Computational engine: glmnet

  add_recipe(weapon_carry_recipe) |>
  add_model(weapon_carry_spec)

title: Lasso Regression
text:
Results and Interpretation
The variable-importance ranking suggests that immediate instability and exposure to violence or victimization are the strongest predictors of adolescent weapon-carrying behavior. Homelessness stands out by a substantial margin as the most influential variable, followed by being attacked in the neighborhood and experiencing parental physical abuse. Parental monitoring also contributes meaningfully, while bullying and sexual abuse by an older person form a second tier of important predictors.
School-related factors, including unfair discipline and school connectedness, appear considerably less influential in the model, while parental substance use and especially parental incarceration contribute relatively little once the other predictors are taken into account.
One important qualification: variable importance measures predictive contribution, not direction or causation. This plot alone does not tell us whether a predictor increases or decreases the likelihood of weapon carrying. For example, the importance of parental monitoring could reflect either low monitoring as a risk factor or high monitoring as a protective factor, depending on how the variable was coded and how the model behaves.
Thus, weapon-carrying behavior was predicted most strongly by homelessness and direct exposure to violence or abuse. Homelessness was substantially more important than any other predictor, followed by neighborhood victimization and parental physical abuse. Parental monitoring, bullying, and sexual abuse also contributed meaningfully, whereas school-related factors, parental substance use, and parental incarceration had comparatively lower predictive importance. However, variable importance reflects predictive contribution and should not be interpreted as indicating either the direction of association or causation.

title: Logistic Regression
text:
Logistic regression is a statistical modeling approach used to estimate the relationship between one or more predictors and a binary outcome. In this analysis, the outcome of interest is whether an adolescent reported carrying a weapon at school. Because the outcome has two possible categories, logistic regression provides a natural framework for estimating how demographic, behavioral, social, and other measured characteristics are associated with the probability of weapon-carrying behavior.
Unlike ordinary linear regression, logistic regression does not model the outcome directly as a continuous value. Instead, it models the log-odds of the outcome and then converts those log-odds into a predicted probability between 0 and 1. This makes it possible to examine both the direction and magnitude of the association between each predictor and the likelihood of weapon carrying while accounting for the other predictors included in the model.
The analysis below uses the 2023 Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS) analytic data and the tidymodels framework in R. The workflow includes data preprocessing, model specification and fitting, coefficient estimation, model evaluation, and visualization of the resulting odds ratios.

Model Overview
Logistic regression is appropriate when the dependent variable is binary, such as 0/1, Yes/No, or True/False. Here, WeaponCarryingSchool is treated as the binary response variable. The model estimates the probability that the outcome is in the event category given a set of predictor variables.
Each regression coefficient represents the estimated change in the log-odds of the outcome associated with a one-unit change in the predictor, holding the other variables constant. Because log-odds are difficult to interpret directly, the coefficients are exponentiated later in the analysis and reported as odds ratios. An odds ratio greater than 1 indicates higher estimated odds of weapon carrying, whereas an odds ratio less than 1 indicates lower estimated odds. An odds ratio close to 1 suggests little association with the outcome after accounting for the remaining predictors.
It is important to interpret these estimates as associations rather than causal effects. The YRBS data are observational, and the model cannot establish that any predictor causes an adolescent to carry a weapon at school.


Implementation
The analysis begins by loading the packages needed for data manipulation, model construction, evaluation, and file-path management. tidymodels supplies the modeling workflow, while tidyverse supports data manipulation and visualization. The dissertation data package and here are also loaded so that the analysis can access the prepared study data in a reproducible way.

library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)
library(dissertationData)
library(here)

# Load and prepare the YRBS 2023 dataset



Load the data
The analysis uses previously prepared data objects rather than repeating the full data-cleaning process here. The full analytic dataset is loaded along with a training set, a test set, and resampling folds. Separating these objects allows the modeling process to distinguish between data used to estimate the model and data reserved for evaluation or resampling.
The training set is used below to fit the logistic regression model. The test set can be used for a more independent assessment of predictive performance, while the fold object supports cross-validation if resampling is incorporated into later model development.

analysis_data <- readRDS(here("models", "data", "analysis_data.rds"))
analysis_train <- readRDS(here("models", "data", "analysis_train.rds"))
analysis_test <- readRDS(here("models", "data", "analysis_test.rds"))
analysis_folds <- readRDS(here("models", "data", "analysis_folds.rds"))



Recipe
A recipe defines the preprocessing steps that will be applied before the model is fit. This is useful because it keeps data preparation tied directly to the modeling workflow and ensures that the same transformations can be reproduced consistently.
The recipe specifies WeaponCarryingSchool as the outcome and includes the remaining variables as predictors. Several preprocessing steps are then applied. Missing categorical values are imputed using the most common category, while missing numeric values are replaced with the corresponding mean. Predictors with zero variance are removed because they contain no information that can help distinguish between outcome categories. Finally, highly correlated numeric predictors are screened using a correlation threshold of 0.70. Removing one variable from strongly correlated pairs can reduce redundancy and improve the stability and interpretability of the fitted coefficients.

weapon_carry_recipe <- 
  recipe(formula = WeaponCarryingSchool ~ ., data = analysis_data) |>
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_mean(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |> 
  step_corr(all_numeric_predictors(), threshold = 0.7)

Bake
After defining the recipe, it is prepared and then applied to the analytic data. In tidymodels, preparing a recipe estimates any quantities needed for preprocessing, such as means for imputation or correlations among predictors. Baking then applies those learned preprocessing steps to a dataset.
The glimpse() output provides a quick check of the resulting variables and their data types. This step is particularly useful for confirming that the recipe behaves as expected before the model is fit.

  prep() %>%

Model Specification
The model specification identifies the type of statistical model to be estimated. logistic_reg() defines a logistic regression model, and the classification mode indicates that the objective is to predict membership in one of two outcome categories. The glm engine uses R’s generalized linear modeling framework to estimate the model.
This is a standard, interpretable logistic regression rather than a heavily tuned machine-learning model. Its primary advantage in this context is that the estimated coefficients can be converted directly to odds ratios and used to describe the adjusted association between each predictor and weapon carrying at school.

weapon_carry_spec <- 
  logistic_reg() %>% 
  set_mode("classification") %>% 
  set_engine("glm") 

weapon_carry_spec

Logistic Regression Model Specification (classification)

Computational engine: glm 




Workflow
The workflow combines the preprocessing recipe and logistic regression specification into a single modeling object. Keeping these steps together helps make the analysis reproducible and reduces the risk that preprocessing will be applied differently at different stages of the modeling process.

weapon_carry_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(weapon_carry_recipe) %>%
  add_model(weapon_carry_spec)

The fitted model coefficients are then converted into a tidy table. Setting exponentiate = TRUE transforms the coefficients from the log-odds scale to odds ratios, which are more intuitive to interpret. The output also includes 95% confidence intervals and p-values for the estimated associations.
For a categorical predictor, an odds ratio compares a particular category with the reference category used by the model. For a numeric predictor, the odds ratio represents the multiplicative change in the odds associated with a one-unit increase in that predictor, unless the variable was transformed beforehand. Confidence intervals provide information about the precision of each estimate. When a 95% confidence interval includes 1, the data are compatible with no adjusted association at the conventional 0.05 significance level.

tidy_model <- 
  mod_1 |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE,
       conf.int = TRUE, 
       conf.level = .95) |>
  mutate(p.value = scales::pvalue(p.value))

Model Evaluation
Model evaluation asks a different question from coefficient interpretation. The regression coefficients describe associations between individual predictors and the outcome, while predictive-performance measures assess how effectively the model distinguishes adolescents who reported weapon carrying at school from those who did not.
The fitted model is first used to generate predictions for the training data. The augmented output includes the observed outcome, the predicted class, and the estimated probability of each outcome category. These probabilities can then be used to evaluate discrimination across different classification thresholds.

weapon_pred <- 
  augment(mod_1, analysis_train) |> 
  select(WeaponCarryingSchool, .pred_class, .pred_1, .pred_0)

weapon_pred

# A tibble: 14,696 × 4
   WeaponCarryingSchool .pred_class .pred_1 .pred_0
   <fct>                <fct>         <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 0                    0            0.0360   0.964
 2 0                    0            0.0412   0.959
 3 0                    0            0.0241   0.976
 4 0                    0            0.0317   0.968
 5 0                    0            0.128    0.872
 6 0                    0            0.0360   0.964

 8 0                    0            0.0201   0.980

10 0                    0            0.0531   0.947
# ℹ 14,686 more rows


The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve summarizes the model’s ability to rank observations according to their predicted probability of the event. The curve compares sensitivity with the false-positive rate across all possible probability thresholds. A model with little discriminatory ability will produce a curve close to the diagonal reference line, while a model with stronger discrimination will bow farther toward the upper-left corner.
The corresponding area under the ROC curve, or AUC, can be interpreted as the probability that the model assigns a higher predicted risk to a randomly selected adolescent with the outcome than to a randomly selected adolescent without the outcome. Values closer to 1 indicate stronger discrimination, while a value near 0.5 indicates performance close to chance.
Because the ROC curve below is calculated on the training data, it primarily describes how well the fitted model separates the observations it was trained on. Predictive performance should generally also be evaluated on the held-out test set or through cross-validation to obtain a less optimistic estimate of how the model is likely to perform on new data.

roc_plot_training <- 
  weapon_pred |> 
  roc_curve(truth = WeaponCarryingSchool, .pred_1, event_level = "second") |> 
  autoplot()

roc_plot_training 










Visualizations
A forest plot provides a compact visual summary of the adjusted odds ratios and their 95% confidence intervals. Each point represents an estimated odds ratio for one predictor, and the horizontal line around the point represents its confidence interval. The vertical dashed line at an odds ratio of 1 represents no association with the outcome.
Predictors plotted to the right of 1 are associated with higher estimated odds of weapon carrying, whereas predictors plotted to the left of 1 are associated with lower estimated odds. The farther an estimate lies from 1, the larger the estimated association on the odds-ratio scale. Confidence intervals should be considered alongside the point estimates: wide intervals indicate greater uncertainty, and intervals that cross 1 do not clearly distinguish the estimated association from no association at the 95% confidence level.
The x-axis is displayed on a logarithmic scale. This is appropriate for odds ratios because values below and above 1 are then represented more symmetrically. For example, an odds ratio of 0.5 and an odds ratio of 2 represent effects of comparable magnitude in opposite directions on the log-odds scale.

tidy_model |> 
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = reorder(term, estimate))) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), height = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "Odds Ratio (log scale)",
    y = "Predictors",
    title = "Forest Plot of Logistic Regression Coefficients"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )

Warning: `geom_errorbarh()` was deprecated in ggplot2 4.0.0.
ℹ Please use the `orientation` argument of `geom_errorbar()` instead.


`height` was translated to `width`.











Results and Interpretation
The fitted logistic regression identified several factors that were independently associated with weapon carrying at school after adjustment for the other predictors included in the model. The forest plot shows considerable variation in both the magnitude and precision of these associations.
Homelessness showed the strongest association with weapon carrying. The estimated odds ratio was approximately 3.2, indicating that adolescents in the category coded 1 for homelessness had more than three times the odds of reporting weapon carrying at school compared with the reference category, holding the other predictors constant. The 95% confidence interval remained well above 1, indicating a comparatively strong and statistically distinguishable association.
Several measures of exposure to violence or adversity were also strongly associated with weapon carrying. Being attacked in the neighborhood was associated with approximately twice the odds of weapon carrying, as was parental physical abuse. Both estimates had confidence intervals entirely above 1. Bullying and sexual abuse by an older person were associated with more moderate increases in the odds of weapon carrying, but their confidence intervals likewise remained above the null value of 1.
Parental monitoring also had an odds ratio substantially above 1. Because the direction of this association depends on how the variable was coded, the substantive interpretation should be made with reference to the original coding of the measure. If the category coded 1 represents lower parental monitoring, for example, the result would indicate that reduced monitoring is associated with greater odds of weapon carrying. This coding should be confirmed before assigning a substantive direction to the association.
Two predictors had odds ratios close enough to 1 that their 95% confidence intervals crossed the null value. Parent incarceration showed only a small positive estimated association, while parent substance use showed an estimated odds ratio below 1. In both cases, however, the confidence intervals included 1. These results therefore provide insufficient evidence of an independent association with weapon carrying after adjustment for the other predictors in this model.
At the other end of the distribution, school connectedness had one of the lowest odds ratios in the model, with its confidence interval entirely below 1. The category coded 1 was therefore associated with substantially lower odds of weapon carrying than the reference category. Unfair discipline at school also had an odds ratio below 1 with a confidence interval that appears to remain below 1. As with parental monitoring, however, the coding of these variables should be verified before describing them substantively as protective or risk factors. The statistical model establishes the direction of the association between the coded categories, not necessarily the direction implied by the variable’s name.
Taken together, the results suggest that experiences involving housing instability, interpersonal violence, and victimization are among the strongest correlates of adolescent weapon carrying in this model. Homelessness stands out in particular, while neighborhood violence, parental physical abuse, bullying, and sexual abuse also retain meaningful associations after simultaneous adjustment for the other included factors.
These estimates should be interpreted as conditional associations rather than causal effects. The analysis shows that these factors are associated with weapon carrying after adjustment for the other measured predictors, but it does not establish that any one factor causes weapon-carrying behavior. Unmeasured confounding, the coding and measurement of survey variables, self-report bias, and the observational nature of the YRBS data should all be considered when interpreting the findings.
The ROC analysis addresses a separate question: how well the predictors collectively distinguish adolescents who reported weapon carrying from those who did not. Accordingly, the coefficient results describe which variables are most strongly associated with the outcome, whereas the ROC curve evaluates the discriminatory performance of the model as a whole.


Key Takeaways
The logistic regression framework allows the relationship between multiple predictors and adolescent weapon carrying at school to be examined simultaneously. The preprocessing recipe addresses missing data, removes predictors that contain no variation, and reduces redundancy among highly correlated numeric variables before model fitting.
The exponentiated model coefficients are interpreted as adjusted odds ratios. Values above 1 indicate higher odds of weapon carrying and values below 1 indicate lower odds, with 95% confidence intervals communicating the uncertainty around those estimates. The forest plot makes these relationships easier to compare visually and helps distinguish large, precise associations from estimates that are smaller or more uncertain.
The ROC analysis provides a separate assessment of the model’s ability to distinguish between adolescents who did and did not report weapon carrying at school. Because the ROC curve shown here is based on the training data, it should be viewed as an in-sample assessment. Evaluation with the held-out test data or cross-validation would provide stronger evidence about the model’s performance on new observations.
Taken together, the analysis is best used to identify and compare factors associated with weapon-carrying behavior and to assess how well those factors collectively discriminate the outcome. The results should not be interpreted as demonstrating that any individual predictor causes weapon carrying.

text:
This website displays a project I worked on during my time at the Summer Institute of Biostatistics and Data Science under the guidance of Dr. Catalina Cañizares. In this project, we explore various statistical and machine learning models using the Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS) 2023 dataset. Through this, I display different implementations and modeling techniques using the tidymodels framework in R.

title: Decision Trees
text: In this note, we check whether a decision tree can predict whether a teen has ever consumed alcohol.

title: Decision Trees
text:
Setup
Like before we load the packages necessary for the analysis.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(MLearnYRBSS)
library(janitor)
library(skimr)
library(vip)
library(rpart.plot)

data("riskyBehaviors")


Recode the outcome
We encode our outcome variable, UseAlcohol, so that it is 0 if a given teen has never used alcohol and 1 if they have used alcohol.

riskyBehaviors_analysis <-
    riskyBehaviors |>
    mutate(
        UsedAlcohol = case_when(
            AgeFirstAlcohol == 1 ~ 0,
            AgeFirstAlcohol %in% c(2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) ~ 1,
            .default = NA
        ),
        UsedAlcohol = factor(UsedAlcohol)
    ) |>
    drop_na(UsedAlcohol) |>
    select(-c(AgeFirstAlcohol, DaysAlcohol, BingeDrinking,
              LargestNumberOfDrinks, SourceAlcohol))

We drop AgeFirstAlcohol, DaysAlcohol, BingeDrinking, LargestNumberOfDrinks, and SourceAlcohol because they are all about alcohol use. If we left them in, the tree would just memorize the answer.


Split + Resample
Here, we stratify the train/test split.

set.seed(2023)

alcohol_split <- initial_split(
    riskyBehaviors_analysis,
    strata = UsedAlcohol
)

alcohol_train <- training(alcohol_split)
alcohol_test <- testing(alcohol_split)

alcohol_split

<Training/Testing/Total>
<9889/3297/13186>


We use strata = to keep the proportion of UsedAlcohol roughly equal in the train and test sets. We use the same logic in the Lasso training. To make sure this worked, we check the class balance:

alcohol_train |>
    tabyl(UsedAlcohol) |>
    adorn_pct_formatting(0) |>
    adorn_totals()

 UsedAlcohol    n percent
           0 4354     44%
           1 5535     56%
       Total 9889       -

alcohol_test |>
    tabyl(UsedAlcohol) |>
    adorn_pct_formatting(0) |>
    adorn_totals()

 UsedAlcohol    n percent
           0 1452     44%
           1 1845     56%
       Total 3297       -


Both sets show the same proportions, meaning strata = did its job.


Cross-validation folds
v = 10 folds of the training set. Every candidate tree we try will be evaluated on all 10 — the test set stays untouched until the very end.

set.seed(2023)

cv_alcohol <- vfold_cv(alcohol_train, v = 10, strata = UsedAlcohol)
cv_alcohol

title: Decision Trees
text:
Workflow

Recipe (preprocessing)
Trees don’t need fancy preprocessing: no step_normalize(), as trees only care about order, not scale; no step_dummy(), as rpart handles factor predictors natively; and imputation is still useful, since rpart can’t split on NA.

alcohol_recipe <-
    recipe(UsedAlcohol ~ ., data = alcohol_train) |>
    step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    step_impute_mean(all_numeric_predictors())

alcohol_recipe

Specification

cart_spec <-
    decision_tree(
        cost_complexity = tune(), # ⬅️ tune
        tree_depth = tune(),      # ⬅️ tune
        min_n = tune()            # ⬅️ tune
    ) |>
    set_engine("rpart") |>
    set_mode("classification")

title: Decision Trees
text:
Tree tuning

Tuning grid
We first set up the tuning grid. Note that levels can be set to 3 for faster turnaround.

tree_grid <- grid_regular(
    cost_complexity(),
    tree_depth(c(2, 5)),
    min_n(),
    levels = 4
)

tree_grid

Run the tuning
Note for those following along that this part can be slow, as there are:

4 × 4 × 4 = 64 candidates
× 10 folds = 640 model fits

We’ll use doParallel to speed it up. Also, we use ROC AUC as the tuning metric — robust to class imbalance, and the same one we used for Lasso.

doParallel::registerDoParallel()

cart_tune <-
    cart_workflow |>
    tune_grid(
        resamples = cv_alcohol,
        grid = tree_grid,
        metrics = metric_set(roc_auc),
        control = control_grid(save_pred = TRUE)
    )

doParallel::stopImplicitCluster()



Show the best candidates
The top 5 hyperparameter combos, ranked by mean ROC AUC across the 10 folds.

Picking the best combination

text:
Evaluate on the Test Set
We use last_fit() to fit all training data to predit on the test set. It computes metrics once, and honestly, with no accidental cheating possible.

cart_last_fit <-
    last_fit(

        split   = alcohol_split,
        metrics = metric_set(accuracy, kap, roc_auc, sensitivity, specificity)
